arXiv:2103.10102v1  [math.DG]  18 Mar 2021
THE BONNET THEOREM FOR ST A TISTICAL MANIFOLDS
TAIJI MARUGAME
Abstract. W e prove the Bonnet theorem for statistical manifolds, whic h
states that if a statistical manifold admits tensors satisf ying the Gauss–Codazzi–
Ricci equations, then it is locally embeddable to a ﬂat stati stical manifold (or
a Hessian manifold). The proof is based on the notion of stati stical embedding
to the product of a vector space and its dual space introduced by Lauritzen. As
another application of Lauritzen’s embedding, we show that a statistical mani-
fold admitting an aﬃne embedding of codimension 1 or 2 is loca lly embeddable
to a ﬂat statistical manifold of the same codimension.
1. Introduction
A statistical manifold ( M, g, ∇ ) is a C∞ -manifold endowed with a Riemannian
metric g and a torsion-free aﬃne connection ∇ such that ∇ g is totally symmetric.
In information geometry, statistical structures naturally appea r as the geometric
structure on the space of probability distributions and play an impor tant role in
the geometric treatment of statistical problems such as statistic al inference (see
[1, 2, 3]).
From the viewpoint of diﬀerential geometry, statistical manifolds c an be consid-
ered as generalization of Riemannian manifolds since a Riemannian manif old with
the Levi-Civita connection ( M, g, ∇ g) is an example of a statistical manifold. How-
ever, there arises a crucial diﬀerence when we consider the notion of “ﬂatness”. A
statistical manifold ( M, g, ∇ ) is called ﬂat when ∇ is a ﬂat connection; we do not
assume that g is a ﬂat metric. Then, the symmetry property of ∇ g imposes that
g is locally the Hessian of a function: g = ∇ 2ψ. Thus, a ﬂat statistical manifold
is equivalent to a so-called Hessian manifold, and its local structure is not unique
unlike the ﬂat models in Riemannian or other Cartan geometries.
In Riemannian geometry, a fundamental problem is the isometric emb edding
problem of Riemannian manifolds into the Euclidean spaces, and one ca n pose the
corresponding problem for statistical manifolds. H. V. Lˆ e [7] solve d this problem
and proved that any statistical manifold can be locally embedded to a ﬂat statistical
manifold of suﬃciently large dimension; see also [3]. This is a statistical a nalogue
of the Nash embedding theorem in Riemannian geometry.
In this paper, we consider a statistical analogue of the Bonnet the orem, which is
a fundamental theorem in the submanifold theory in Riemannian geom etry. A sub-
manifold in the Euclidean space inherits the induced metric (the ﬁrst f undamental
form) and an extrinsic curvature called the second fundamental f orm. These quanti-
ties satisfy algebraic and diﬀerential equations called the Gauss–Co dazzi equations.
The classical Bonnet theorem asserts that conversely if a Riemann ian manifold ad-
mits tensors with the Gauss–Codazzi equations, then it is locally emb edded iso-
metrically to the Euclidean space. For a submanifold of a ﬂat statistic al manifold,
we can also deﬁne the induced statistical structure ( g, ∇ ) and extrinsic curvature
2010 Mathematics Subject Classiﬁcation. Primary 53B12, Secondary 53B25.
Key words and phrases. statistical manifolds; Hessian manifolds; the Gauss–Coda zzi–Ricci
equations; the Bonnet theorem.

of this paper is to prove the following Bonnet theorem for statistica l manifolds:
Theorem 1.1. Let (M, g, ∇ ) be an n-dimensional statistical manifold and r a
positive integer. If there exist tensors
(ha

which satisfy the Gauss–Codazzi–Ricci equations (3.3), then M is locally embeddable
to a ﬂat statistical manifold of dimension n + r.
As noted above, the local structure of ﬂat statistical manifolds is not unique and
this prevents us from applying straightforwardly the standard te chnique of prov-
ing Bonnet-type theorems. We overcome this diﬃculty by invoking th e notion of
statistical embedding to the product of mutually dual vector spac e V × V ∗ , intro-
duced by Lauritzen [6]. A key step in the proof of Theorem 1.1 is to est ablish that
the embeddability to V × V ∗ in the sense of Lauritzen is in fact locally equivalent
to the embeddability to a ﬂat statistical manifold (Theorem 2.2). This equiva-
lence has an immediate application to the embeddability of statistical s tructures
(g, ∇ (α)) ( α ∈ R); see Proposition 2.3.
We also have an application of Theorem 2.2 to aﬃne embeddings of stat istical
manifolds. There have been studies of statistical manifolds from th e viewpoint
of aﬃne diﬀerential geometry ([9]). There is a notion of embedding of statistical
manifolds to aﬃne spaces of codimension 1 , 2 and the aﬃne embeddability is closely
related to the generalized conformal structures on statistical m anifolds ([4, 5, 8]).
However, in the aﬃne embedding, the metric g is deﬁned by the second fundamental
form instead of the induced metric, so its relation to the usual stat istical embedding
is not clear at once. In this paper, we prove that the aﬃne embedda bility implies
the embeddablity to a ﬂat statistical manifold:
Theorem 1.2. Let r = 1 , 2. If an n-dimensional statistical manifold (M, g, ∇ )
admits a local aﬃne embedding to Rn+r, then it is locally embeddable to a ﬂat
statistical manifold of dimension n + r.
The proof is given by the application of Theorem 2.2 to the pair of the a ﬃne
embedding and its dual (conormal) embedding.
This paper is organized as follows: In §2, we review some notions on statistical
manifolds and prove the equivalence (Theorem 2.2) of the usual emb eddability to
a ﬂat statistical manifold and that of Lauritzen. Then, we apply this fact to aﬃne
embeddings and prove Theorem 1.2. In §3, we deﬁne extrinsic curvature quantities
on submanifolds in a ﬂat statistical manifold and derive the Gauss–Co dazzi–Ricci
equations. Finally, we prove the Bonnet theorem (Theorem 1.1) bas ed on Theorem
2.2.
Notations: We adopt Einstein’s summation convention. The indices i, j, k, l are
used for tensors on the (sub)manifold M and run from 1 to n. The indices A, B, K, L
are used for tensors on the ambient space S or V and run from 1 to N (= n + r).
The indices a, b, c are used for complementary directions to M and run from 1 to
r(= N − n). The skew symmetrization of indices are denoted by [ , ] and performed
only over indices such as i, j, k. For example,

2. Statistical manifolds
2.1. Statistical structures. We will brieﬂy review some basic notions on statis-
tical manifolds; we refer the reader to the books [2, 3] for details.
Let M be an n-dimensional C∞ -manifold. We call ( g, ∇ ) a statistical structure if
g is a Riemannian metric and ∇ is a torsion-free aﬃne connection on M such that
∇ g is a totally symmetric 3-tensor: ∇ [igj]k = 0. We lower and raise the indices
by the metric gij and its inverse gij. The dual connection ∇ ∗ of ∇ is the aﬃne
connection characterized by the equation
X ·g(Y, Z ) = g(∇ X Y, Z ) + g(Y, ∇ ∗
XZ), X, Y, Z ∈ Γ(T M).
The condition that ∇ g is totally symmetric is equivalent to saying that ∇ ∗ is also
torsion-free. Thus, ( g, ∇ ∗ ) also becomes a statistical structure, which is called the
dual statistical structure . Since ∇ and ∇ ∗ are torsion-free, their curvature tensors
are given by the Ricci identities
(∇ i∇ j − ∇ j ∇ i)X k = Rij
k

It is easy to show that R and R∗ are related by
(2.1) Rijkl = − R∗
ijlk .
We also have a 1-parameter family of statistical structure ( g, ∇ (α)), α ∈ R, where
the α-connection ∇ (α) is deﬁned by
∇ (α) := 1 + α
2 ∇ + 1 − α
2 ∇ ∗ .
The dual connection of ∇ (α) is equal to ∇ (− α) and since both connections are
torsion-free, ( g, ∇ (α)) is indeed a statistical structure.
2.2. Flat statistical structures. A statistical structure ( g, ∇ ) is said to be ﬂat
when ∇ is a ﬂat connection: Rij kl = 0. In this case, the dual connection is also ﬂat
by the equation (2.1), so we also call ( g, ∇ , ∇ ∗ ) a dually ﬂat structure . Although
the metric g may not be ﬂat, the condition ∇ [igj]k = 0 and the Poincar´ e lemma
imply that locally one can write as
gij = ∇ i∇ j ψ
with some function ψ. Conversely, if ∇ is ﬂat and g is locally written as the
Hessian of a function, then ( g, ∇ ) becomes a ﬂat statistical structure. Thus, the
ﬂat statistical structure is equivalent to the Hessian structure .
Let ( ξ1, . . . , ξn) be local aﬃne coordinates for ∇ , and ψ a Hesse potential of g:
∇ ∂

ηi := ∂ψ

Then, ( η1, . . . , ηn) become aﬃne coordinates for ∇ ∗ , called the dual coordinates,
and ψ gives a Hesse potential of g with respect to ∇ ∗ . Moreover, we have

2.3. Statistical submanifolds and statistical embeddings. Let ( S, G, D) be
a statistical manifold and M ⊂ S a submanifold. Then, we can deﬁne a statistical
structure ( g, ∇ ) on M by setting
g(X, Y ) = G(X, Y ), g (∇ X Y, Z ) = G(DX Y, Z )
for X, Y, Z ∈ Γ(T M). In other words, the metric g is deﬁned by the restriction
of G and the connection ∇ is the “orthogonal projection” of D with respect to
G. One can see that ∇ is torsion-free and the dual connection ∇ ∗ is given by
g(∇ ∗
X Y, Z ) = G(D∗
X Y, Z ). Thus, ∇ ∗ is also torsion-free, so ( g, ∇ ) is a statistical
structure.
Let ( M, g, ∇ ), ( S, G, D) be two statistical manifolds, and f : M − → S an em-
bedding. We say f is a statistical embedding if ( g, ∇ ) agrees with the statistical
structure induced on f (M ) ⊂ S when we identify M with its image f (M ). In this
paper, we only consider local embeddings to ﬂat statistical manifold s. When we say
(M, g, ∇ ) is locally embeddable to a ﬂat statistical manifold , we mean that for any
point x ∈ M , there exist an open neighborhood U of x, a ﬂat statistical manifold
(S, G, D), and a statistical embedding f : U − → S .
2.4. Lauritzen’s statistical embedding. Lauritzen [6] introduced another no-
tion of statistical embedding whose target space is the product of two mutually
dual vector spaces instead of a ﬂat statistical manifold (see also [2 ]):
Deﬁnition 2.1. Let (M, g, ∇ ) be a statistical manifold, and V a real vector space.
A pair of embeddings
(f, ϕ) : M − → V × V ∗
is called a statistical embedding (in the sense of Lauritzen) if
(2.2) g(X, Y ) = ⟨f∗ X, ϕ∗ Y ⟩, g (∇ X Y, Z ) = ⟨X ·f∗ Y, ϕ∗ Z⟩
hold for any X, Y, Z ∈ Γ(T M), where ⟨ , ⟩ denotes the natural paring of V and V ∗ .
In the equation (2.2), we are identifying each tangent space TξV or TηV ∗ with
V or V ∗ , so f∗ X and ϕ∗ Y are regarded as V -valued or V ∗ -valued functions on M .
In the index notation, we can express (2.2) as
gij = (∂if A)(∂jϕA), Γijk (= gklΓij l) = ( ∂i∂jf A)(∂kϕA).
We note that the mapping
(ϕ, f) : M − → V ∗ × V
gives a statistical embedding of the dual statistical manifold ( M, g, ∇ ∗ ).
The following theorem asserts that the two notions of statistical e mbedding are
locally equivalent:
Theorem 2.2. Let (M, g, ∇ ) be an n-dimensional statistical manifold. Then the
following are equivalent:
(i) M is locally embeddable to an N -dimensional ﬂat statistical manifold.
(ii) M is locally embeddable to V × V ∗ in the sense of Lauritzen for an N -
dimensional vector space V .
Proof. First we prove (i) ⇒ (ii). Let ( S, G, D) be an N -dimensional ﬂat statistical
manifold, and suppose F : M − → S is a statistical embedding deﬁned on a neigh-
borhood of a point. (For simplicity, we also denote the neighborhood by M .) We
take local aﬃne coordinates ( ξA) for D and a Hesse potential ψ for G, and denote
the dual coordinates by ( ηA):
G = ∂2ψ
∂ξ A∂ξ B dξA ⊗ dξB, η A = ∂ψ
∂ξ A .

Thus, f : M − → V is a statistical embedding. □
As an application of Theorem 2.2, we will prove the following
Proposition 2.3. If a statistical manifold (M, g, ∇ ) is locally embeddable to an
N -dimensional ﬂat statistical manifold, then (M, g, ∇ (α)), α ∈ R, are locally em-
beddable to a ﬂat statistical manifold of dimension 2N .
Proof. By Theorem 2.2, we have a local statistical embedding ( f, ϕ) : (M, g, ∇ ) − →
V × V ∗ for an N -dimensional vector space V . For each α ∈ R, we deﬁne a mapping
(F, Φ) : M − → (V ⊕ V ∗ ) × (V ∗ ⊕ V )
by
F :=
(

2 ϕ
)
, Φ :=
( 1 + α

.

⟨F∗ X, Φ∗Y ⟩ = 1 + α
2 g(X, Y ) + 1 − α
2 g(Y, X ) = g(X, Y ),
⟨X ·F∗ Y, Φ∗Z⟩ = 1 + α
2 g(∇ X Y, Z ) + 1 − α
2 g(∇ ∗
X Y, Z ) = g(∇ (α)
X Y, Z ).
Hence (F, Φ) is a statistical embedding, and by Theorem 2.2, ( M, g, ∇ (α)) is locally
embeddable to a ﬂat statistical manifold of dimension dim( V ⊕ V ∗ ) = 2 N . □
2.5. Aﬃne embeddings of statistical manifolds: proof of Theorem 1.2.
We can also use Theorem 2.2 to prove Theorem 1.2, which gives a relatio n between
statistical embeddings and aﬃne embeddings.
Let M be an n-dimensional C∞ -manifold. First we consider the aﬃne embedding
of codimension 1. Let f : M − → Rn+1 be an embedding, and ξ ∈ Γ(f ∗ T Rn+1) a
transverse vector ﬁeld. Then, according to the decomposition f ∗ T Rn+1 = f∗ T M ⊕
Rξ, we can write as
DX (f∗ Y ) = f∗ (∇ X Y ) − g(X, Y )ξ,
DX ξ = f∗ (S(X)) + τ (X)ξ
for X, Y ∈ Γ(T M), where D denotes the canonical ﬂat connection on f ∗T Rn+1.
One can see that ∇ deﬁnes a torsion-free aﬃne connection on M , and g gives a
symmetric 2-tensor, called the aﬃne second fundamental form . The endomorphism
S is called the aﬃne shape operator . These quantities satisfy the Gauss–Codazzi–
Ricci equations derived from the ﬂatness of D, and it follows that ( g, ∇ ) gives a
statistical structure on M if g is positive deﬁnite and τ = 0 (equiaﬃne condition).
In this case, we say the statistical manifold ( M, g, ∇ ) admits an aﬃne embedding to
Rn+1. Dillen–Nomizu–Vrankan [4] proved the aﬃne Bonnet theorem, which states
that if a statistical manifold has tensors with the Gauss–Codazzi–R icci equations,
then it admits an aﬃne embedding to Rn+1. Moreover, they showed that the
embeddability is also characterized by the condition that the statist ical structure
is 1-conformally ﬂat , or equivalently the dual connection ∇ ∗ is projectively ﬂat; see
also [5].
When a statistical manifold M admits an aﬃne embedding {f, ξ} as above, it
also has the dual embedding or the conormal mapping ϕ : M − → (Rn+1)∗ deﬁned
by
ϕ(x)|f∗ TxM = 0, ⟨ξx, ϕ(x)⟩ = 1.
Since τ = 0, ϕ satisﬁes
(2.5) ⟨ξ, ϕ∗ Z⟩ = Z · ⟨ξ, ϕ⟩ − ⟨ DZ ξ, ϕ⟩ = 0 for Z ∈ Γ(T M).

Using this, we have
(2.6)
⟨f∗ X, ϕ∗ Y ⟩ = Y · ⟨f∗ X, ϕ⟩ − ⟨ DY (f∗ X), ϕ⟩ = g(X, Y ),
⟨X ·f∗ Y, ϕ∗ Z⟩ = ⟨f∗ (∇ X Y ), ϕ∗ Z⟩ = g(∇ X Y, Z ).
Note that by the ﬁrst equation, ϕ∗ is injective so ϕ is a local embedding. These
two equations imply that the pair ( f, ϕ) : M − → Rn+1 × (Rn+1)∗ is a statistical
embedding in the sense of Lauritzen. This proves Theorem 1.2 in the c ase of
codimension 1.
Next we consider aﬃne embeddings of codimension 2. Let f : M − → Rn+2 be
an embedding of an n-dimensional C∞ -manifold. We assume that the position
vector ﬁeld η = xA(∂/∂x A) ∈ Γ(f ∗ T Rn+2) is transverse to f∗ T M. Supplying
one more transverse vector ﬁeld ξ ∈ Γ(f ∗ T Rn+2), we consider the decomposition
f ∗ T Rn+2 = f∗T M ⊕ Rξ ⊕ Rη. For X, Y ∈ Γ(T M), we write as
DX (f∗ Y ) = f∗ (∇ X Y ) − g(X, Y )ξ − k(X, Y )η,
DXξ = f∗ (S(X)) + τ (X)ξ + µ(X)η,
DXη = X.
Again, ( g, ∇ ) deﬁnes a statistical structure on M if g is positive deﬁnite and τ = 0,
and we say that the statistical manifold ( M, g, ∇ ) admits an aﬃne embedding of
codimension 2. Matsuzoe [8] proved that the aﬃne embeddability of c odimension 2
is characterized by the condition that ( g, ∇ ) is conformally-projectively ﬂat, which
is a generalization of the 1-conformally ﬂatness.
For an aﬃne embedding f of codimension 2, we can also deﬁne the dual embed-
ding ϕ : M − → (Rn+2)∗ by
ϕ(x)|f∗TxM⊕ Rηx = 0, ⟨ξx, ϕ(x)⟩ = 1.
Then, we again have the equation (2.5) and
⟨η, ϕ∗ Z⟩ = Z · ⟨η, ϕ⟩ − ⟨ DZ η, ϕ⟩ = 0 for Z ∈ Γ(T M).
Consequently, we obtain (2.6) as well, and ( f, ϕ) : M − → Rn+2 × (Rn+2)∗ gives a
statistical embedding in the sense of Lauritzen. Thus we have prov ed Theorem 1.2
in the case of codimension 2.
3. The Bonnet theorem
3.1. The Gauss–Codazzi–Ricci equations for statistical embedd ings. Let
(M, g, ∇ ) be an n-dimensional statistical manifold and ( S, G, D) an N -dimensional
ﬂat statistical manifold. For a statistical embedding f : M − → S , we will deﬁne
extrinsic curvature quantities and diﬀerential equations satisﬁed by them.
We set r := N − n and let ( νa) = ( ν1, . . . , νr) be a local orthonormal frame
for ( f∗ T M)⊥ ⊂ f ∗ T S with respect to G. Then, locally we have the orthogonal
decomposition
f ∗ T S = f∗ T M ⊕ R
r,
where Rr := M × Rr is the trivial bundle deﬁned by ( νa). In calculations with the
index notation, it is convenient to identify Rr with its dual ( Rr)∗ and regard ( νa) as
a frame of ( Rr)∗ as well as Rr; thus we also write νa for νa under this identiﬁcation.
For vector ﬁelds X, Y ∈ Γ(T M), we can write as
DXY = f∗ (∇ X Y ) − ha(X, Y )νa,
DX νa = f∗ (Sa(X)) + τ b

We will derive the Gauss–Codazzi–Ricci equations for these tensor s from the

3.2. The statistical Bonnet theorem: proof of Theorem 1.1. We will prove
the Bonnet theorem for statistical manifold (Theorem 1.1). Suppo se that an n-
dimensional statistical manifold ( M, g, ∇ ) admits tensors ha
ij, h ∗
aij, τ a
bi satisfying
the equations (3.3). By Theorem 2.2, it suﬃces to construct a local statistical
embedding f : M − → Rn+r × (Rn+r)∗ in the sense of Lauritzen.
We consider the vector bundle E := T M ⊕ R
r and deﬁne linear connections
∇ , ∇ ∗ on E by (3.1). By a direct computation, we see that these are dual to ea ch
other with respect to the ﬁber metric G deﬁned by (3.2). Moreover, the Gausss–
Codazzi–Ricci equations (3.3) imply that both connections are ﬂat. Hence we can
take local frames ( eA), (e∗
A) of E which are parallel with respect to these connec-
tions: ∇ eA = ∇ ∗ e∗
A = 0. Since G(eA, e∗
B) is constant, we can choose ( eA), (e∗
A) so
that
(3.4) G(eA, e∗
B) = δAB.
Let F : E − → M × Rn+r be the local trivialization by the frame ( eA) and deﬁne a
local Rn+r-valued 1-form θ on M by
θ(X) := F
( ( X
0
) )
, X ∈ Γ(T M).
We will show that θ is a closed form. For X, Y ∈ Γ(T M), we have
F

F

0

It then follows that
dθ(X, Y ) = X ·θ(Y ) − Y ·θ(X) − θ([X, Y ])
= θ(∇ X Y − ∇ Y X − [X, Y ])
= 0
as ∇ is torsion-free. Thus, θ is closed and locally we can write as θ = d f with a
mapping f : M − → Rn+r. Similarly, by using the local trivialization by the frame
(e∗
A), we deﬁne θ∗ = dϕ, ϕ : M − → (Rn+r)∗ ; in this case we regard the ﬁber as the
